sections.title: The Power of Questions
sections.content: Socratic questioning uses a sequence of designed questions to lead your opponent to contradict themselves.
bullets: Closed questions force a Yes/No commitment
Leading questions suggest the desired answer
A 3-question trap can dismantle a complex argument

sections.title: Building a Question Trap
sections.content: Establish common ground, Apply the principle, Reveal the contradiction.
bullets: Step 1: 'Would you agree that protecting children is a government priority?' (Yes)
Step 2: 'Would you agree that social media algorithms expose children to harm?' (Yes)
Step 3: 'Then why oppose regulating those algorithms?' (Contradiction)

sections.title: A 3-Question Trap
sections.good:
Q1: 'Do you agree minimizing unnecessary suffering is a moral obligation?' (Yes)
Q2: 'Do you agree alternatives exist?' (Yes)
Q3: 'Then why allow testing when alternatives exist?'
sections.explanation: Each question builds on the previous. By Q3, the opponent's position contradicts their own values.

sections.instruction: Which question type forces a simple 'Yes' or 'No'?
sections.feedback: Closed questions limit the opponent to Yes or No.

sections.q: What is the purpose of the first question in a Socratic trap?
options: To establish a general principle the opponent will agree with
sections.explain: The first question establishes common ground. Once agreed, apply it to the debate.

sections.statement: Socratic questioning is manipulative and should not be used in fair debate.
sections.feedback: It is a legitimate logical tool that exposes inconsistencies in reasoning.
